Generate a self-contained, reproducible R script from a specification

Source: R/spec_builder.R
generate_r_script.Rd

Embed the specification as the JSON text that spec_json() writes, so that the returned script reproduces the design without any external file. This turns a design built in the no-code application into a reproducible script. The application's Verify button runs that script in a clean R session and checks that its data are identical, bit for bit, to the data the application's current specification produces.

Usage

generate_r_script(spec)

Arguments

spec

A design specification (list), as produced by build_spec(), or the path of a specification file for load_spec() to read.

Value

A length-one character string containing a runnable R script that loads pilotr, embeds the specification and simulates the data, with the installation line and the suggested analysis as comments.

Details

The script ends with a commented suggestion of the analysis that fits the design. A two-group Gaussian design with one row per subject is sent to power_design(), whose t-test takes no other. An ordinal or beta outcome is sent to generate_design_analysis(), which writes a Bayesian design analysis on the link scale to design_analysis.R, since power_mixed() fits such an outcome only on the response scale. Any other design is sent to power_mixed(), and only then does the installation line name lme4 and lmerTest, which it needs.

Since the point of the script is bit-for-bit reproduction, the embedded specification has to preserve every coefficient exactly. The JSON text sits in a raw string that load_spec() reads with 'jsonlite', which parses numbers with the C library's strtod(). That rounds correctly, so each number reaches the script as the double it was on every build of R, and the numbers stay as readable as in the specification file. Written as R literals, they would be left to R's own parser. On a build without long-double arithmetic, such as R on Apple silicon, that parser can read a 17-digit decimal one unit in the last place away. deparse() is no alternative either, since it prints 15 significant digits and deparse(1/3) reads back as a different double.

Examples

spec <- build_spec(list(name = "demo", seed = 1, design_kind = "between",
  factor_name = "group", lev1 = "a", lev2 = "b", n_subject = 20,
  intercept = 0, effect = 0.5, family = "gaussian", resp_name = "", sigma = 1))
cat(generate_r_script(spec))
#> # Reproducible simulation exported by pilotr.
#> # install.packages("pilotr")   # from CRAN
#> library(pilotr)
#> 
#> # The specification as spec_json() writes it. load_spec() reads it with jsonlite, which
#> # recovers every number exactly on every build of R.
#> spec <- load_spec(r"(
#> {
#>   "spec_version": "0.3",
#>   "name": "demo",
#>   "seed": 1,
#>   "units": {
#>     "subject": {
#>       "n": 20
#>     }
#>   },
#>   "factors": [
#>     {
#>       "name": "group",
#>       "levels": ["a", "b"],
#>       "contrasts": {
#>         "effect": [-0.5, 0.5]
#>       },
#>       "between": "subject"
#>     }
#>   ],
#>   "fixed": {
#>     "intercept": 0,
#>     "coefficients": {
#>       "effect": 0.5
#>     }
#>   },
#>   "response": {
#>     "family": "gaussian",
#>     "name": "score",
#>     "sigma": 1,
#>     "round": 4
#>   }
#> }
#> )")
#> 
#> data <- simulate_design(spec)              # analysis-ready data frame
#> # write.csv(data, "data.csv", row.names = FALSE)
#> # pow <- power_design(spec, n_sims = 1000)   # power with Type S and Type M
